newsitem.title: USA: Komag expects weak results for rest of year.
newsitem.headline: Komag expects weak results for rest of year.

text.p: Komag Inc. warned Wednesday that results for its second quarter and the rest of its fiscal year would fall short of expectations due to weak demand for disk drives.

Komag, which makes thin-film media used to store data on computer hard disk drives, said in a statement it expects to earn less in its second quarter ending June 29 than the 33 cents a share it made in its first quarter. Komag said sales would be slightly higher than the $167.2 million in the first quarter.

Analysts had expected the San Jose-based company to earn 45 cents a share in the second quarter, according to First Call. In the comparable year-ago quarter Komag had profits of $42.5 million, or 80 cents a share.

The company attributed the shortfall to weak demand for very large disk drives and lower-than-expected production levels. Komag said second-quarter gross margins would fall slightly below the 23.5 percent reported for the first quarter. It also said its 50 percent-owned Japanese joint venture, Asahi Komag Co. Ltd., will post a second-quarter loss due to product transitions.

Orders from Seagate Technology Inc., the biggest disk drive maker in the world, will be cut in half to about 15 percent of sales compared to the first quarter, Komag said. The company had expected Seagate's orders to rise for the rest of the fiscal year.

The company said because of the lower Seagate orders it will have excess production capacity which will cause gross margins and earnings for the third and fourth fiscal quarter to fall below first and second quarter levels.

"The replacement of lost Seagate orders is critical to our second-half financial performance," Komag President Stephen Johnson said. "Unfortunately, the currently anticipated level of order replacement will be insufficient to fully utilize our expanded second-half production capacity."
Komag said it is is reviewing plans for $290 million in capital expenditures during fiscal 1997 in light of the weaker results. It may also take other actions to cut spending, it said.
The company said it has adequate financial flexibility, with $200 million available under its recently expanded credit lines and a cash balance of about $80 million.
